finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but ignores its boolean return value (it is not require_edit), so the authorization check is never enforced. Any authenticated user can overwrite the body of any document they do not own or edit.
finding.source: PUT /doc/<doc_id> with JSON {"body": ...} from any authenticated user (g.user) who is not owner or editor; doc_id is attacker-chosen
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20 (write to the protected document)

trace.note: route PUT /doc/<doc_id>, no auth decorator or guard
doc loaded by request-supplied id with no ownership check
can_edit(g.user, doc) returns False but the result is discarded; no if/abort

finding.guards_checked: Compared with update_title (line 27), which correctly uses require_edit and aborts with 403. can_edit (line 7) only returns a bool. No before_request hook or middleware exists in the file that sets or enforces g.user or ownership. How g.user is populated is not defined here, so any identity-based enforcement upstream is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: can_edit (docs.py:7) returns a bool only and its result is discarded at line 19; require_edit (line 11) aborts with 403 but is only used in update_title. No before_request/login_required/g.user setup exists in the directory.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit() as a bare statement with its bool result discarded, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any caller, unlike update_title at docs.py:27 which uses require_edit and aborts with 403.
